candidates.quote: I never saw daffodils so beautiful. They grew among the mossy stones about and above them; some rested their heads upon these stones, as on a pillow, for weariness; and the rest tossed and reeled and danced, and seemed as if they verily laughed with the wind, that blew upon them over the lake; they looked so gay, ever glancing, ever changing.
candidates.author: Dorothy Wordsworth
candidates.work: The Grasmere Journal, in Journals of Dorothy Wordsworth
candidates.locator: Entry of Thursday 15th (April 1802), on the shore of Ullswater beyond Gowbarrow Park; Journals of Dorothy Wordsworth, ed. William Knight (Macmillan, 1897), vol. I, p. 106, read in the Wikisource transcription of that scan. Knight regularises the manuscript: the later editions (Darbishire, Moorman, Pamela Woof) print ampersands and about and about them, so this wording is Knight’s and the source must name his edition.
candidates.whyThisMonth: The fifteenth of April in a notebook: the flowers are already doing what the month is for, and the reader is asked to do nothing but go and look at them.

candidates.quote: I was brought up in a distant province which lies farther than the farthest end of the Eastern Road.
candidates.author: Lady Sarashina
candidates.locator: The opening sentence; Diaries of Court Ladies of Old Japan, trans. Annie Shepley Omori and Kochi Doi (Houghton Mifflin, 1920), where the diary is the first of the three and begins at p. 1; read in the archive.org scan cu31924023323623. The author is known only as the daughter of Sugawara no Takasue; Ivan Morris’s 1971 version, As I Crossed a Bridge of Dreams, renders the sentence differently, so the translation must be named.
candidates.whyThisMonth: A diary that opens at the far end of a road and is made of journeys afterwards puts the reader at the start of the way, which is where April wants them.
candidates.translator: Annie Shepley Omori and Kochi Doi, 1920

candidates.quote: Life is what we make of it. Travel is the traveller. What we see isn’t what we see but what we are.
candidates.author: Fernando Pessoa
candidates.locator: In the text on what travel is good for, a few lines after the question about new sensations; trans. Richard Zenith, read in the archive.org scans bookofdisquiet0000pess (Penguin, New York, 2003) and bookofdisquietud0000soar (The Book of Disquietude, Sheep Meadow Press, 1996), both of which read traveller. Secondary citations number the text 451 and give p. 371 of the 2002 Penguin: the number and the page are reported, not seen, and must be checked on the page.
candidates.speaker: Bernardo Soares, the assistant bookkeeper in whose voice the book is written
candidates.whyThisMonth: For a month of setting out it says the plain thing about the road: it gives back the person who walks it, so it matters who sets off this morning.

candidates.quote: Life shrinks or expands in proportion to one’s courage.
candidates.author: Anaïs Nin
candidates.work: The Diary of Anaïs Nin, Volume Three: 1939 to 1944
candidates.locator: A one sentence paragraph in the entries headed [June, 1941], which open at p. 120 of the Harcourt, Brace and World edition, ed. Gunther Stuhlmann (1969); it follows the sentence about a friend who showed no feeling. Read in the archive.org scan diaryofanaisnin0003nina and confirmed in four other printings; the page of the line itself was not seen, so the page number is still to be fixed.
candidates.whyThisMonth: It makes the size of a day a question of nerve rather than of circumstance, which is the useful thing to hear before the day has started.
candidates.year: 1969 (the volume); the entry is of June 1941

candidates.quote: But let us open our leaves like a flower, and be passive and receptive; budding patiently under the eye of Apollo and taking hints from every noble insect that favours us with a visit.
candidates.author: John Keats
candidates.work: Letters of John Keats to His Family and Friends
candidates.locator: Letter XXXVII, to John Hamilton Reynolds, Hampstead, 19 February 1818, the letter that carries the thrush’s song; ed. Sidney Colvin (Macmillan, 1891), read in Project Gutenberg 35698. Colvin runs on after visit with a dash and Sap will be given us for meat, and dew for drink: the sentence is cut there and given a full stop. Four sentences later Keats says he was led into these thoughts by the beauty of the morning.
candidates.whyThisMonth: Written on a spring morning by a man who had read nothing that day and thought the morning was right, it gives the reader leave to open slowly instead of chasing.

candidates.quote: And I’ve grasped some solid and useful things in drawing and in painting, more firmly than you think, my dear friend. But I keep on making what I can’t do yet in order to learn to be able to do it.
candidates.author: Vincent van Gogh
candidates.locator: Letter 528 (R57 in the old numbering), to Anthon van Rappard, Nuenen, on or about Tuesday 18 August 1885; the scholarly edition ed. Leo Jansen, Hans Luijten and Nienke Bakker (Van Gogh Museum and Huygens ING, 2009), read at vangoghletters.org/vg/letters/let528. The line travels in a smoother form that is usually pinned on Picasso, so the Van Gogh Museum wording is the one to print.
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is the plainest statement of the road that teaches: you go on making the thing you cannot do yet, and that is how the doing arrives.
candidates.translator: the Van Gogh Museum edition, 2009 (English coordinated by Michael Hoyle; translators include Sue Dyson, Imogen Forster and Lynne Richards)

candidates.quote: To-day I made the ascent of the highest mountain in this region, which is not improperly called Ventosum. My only motive was the wish to see what so great an elevation had to offer.
candidates.author: Petrarch
candidates.work: Letter to Dionisio da Borgo San Sepolcro, known as The Ascent of Mount Ventoux (Familiares IV, 1)
candidates.locator: The opening sentences; Petrarch: The First Modern Scholar and Man of Letters, trans. James Harvey Robinson with Henry Winchester Rolfe (G. P. Putnam, 1898), pp. 307 to 308, read in the Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook text, which carries Robinson’s page marks. The letter is signed Malaucene, April 26; the traditional date is 1336, and scholars hold that Petrarch wrote it up considerably later.
candidates.whyThisMonth: A man climbs a mountain in April for no reason except to see what is up there, and says so in his first line: the month’s own impulse, six centuries early.
candidates.translator: James Harvey Robinson and Henry Winchester Rolfe, 1898

candidates.quote: I often say, when I make these little observations, ‘Had Aristotle cooked, he would have written a great deal more.’
candidates.author: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
candidates.work: The Answer (La Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz)
candidates.locator: In the passage on the secrets of nature she has learned while cooking, a few lines after what can we women know, save philosophies of the kitchen?; The Answer / La Respuesta, trans. Electa Arenal and Amanda Powell (The Feminist Press, 1994), read in the archive.org scans answerincludings0000juan and answerlarespuest00sorj. One printing sets the inner quotation with single marks and one with double: the printed page decides which the card uses.
candidates.whyThisMonth: It hands the reader the ordinary work of the day as the place where knowledge is actually made, which is the road that teaches in its most domestic form.

candidates.quote: Spring is the time of plans and projects.
candidates.author: Leo Tolstoy
candidates.locator: Part Two, chapter 13, opening the paragraph in which Levin goes out to his farm after the thaw; trans. Constance Garnett (Heinemann, 1901), read in Project Gutenberg 1399. The sentence continues: and, as he came out into the farmyard, Levin, like a tree in spring that knows not what form will be taken by the young shoots and twigs imprisoned in its swelling buds, hardly knew what undertakings he was going to begin upon.
candidates.whyThisMonth: The season itself is the planning season, and at six in the morning the plan can still be made before the hours are spoken for.

candidates.quote: One day, as he followed the course of a stream, he became unconscious of the distance he had travelled. All at once he came upon a grove of blossoming peach trees which lined either bank for hundreds of paces.
candidates.author: Tao Yuanming
candidates.locator: The second and third sentences, just after the fisherman of Wu-ling is introduced; Anthology of Chinese Literature, Volume I: From Early Times to the Fourteenth Century, ed. and trans. Cyril Birch (Grove Press, 1965), pp. 167 to 168, read in the Columbia Asia for Educators reprint of those pages, which carries Birch’s translation with permission.
candidates.whyThisMonth: The oldest account of what a walk can do: he loses count of the distance and the blossom begins, which is the whole argument for going outdoors in April.

candidates.quote: When I left Queen’s my future seemed to stretch out before me like a straight road. I thought I could see along it for many a milestone. Now there is a bend in it. I don’t know what lies around the bend, but I’m going to believe that the best does.
candidates.author: L. M. Montgomery
candidates.locator: Chapter XXXVIII, The Bend in the Road, in the speech where Anne gives up the Redmond scholarship to stay at Green Gables; L. C. Page, 1908, read in Project Gutenberg 45, which follows the first edition. The page of the 1908 printing is still to be fixed, as the landed January line was fixed to p. 247.
candidates.speaker: Anne Shirley, to Marilla Cuthbert
candidates.whyThisMonth: For the morning when the plan has changed: the road bends, nobody can see past the bend, and she decides in advance that what is round it is good.

candidates.quote: All the same I’m not going to accept your kind invitation, for the time being at any rate. The reason is that my pink cactus is probably going to flower. It’s a very rare plant I’ve been given, and I’m told that in our climate it flowers only once every four years.
candidates.author: Colette
candidates.work: Break of Day (La Naissance du jour)
candidates.locator: The letter from the narrator’s mother that opens the book, pp. 5 to 6; Break of Day, trans. Enid McLeod (Farrar, Straus and Cudahy, 1961), read in the archive.org scan breakofdaynovel0000cole, where the narrator’s I am the daughter of the woman who wrote that letter follows on p. 6. Colette’s biographers note that the letter Sido actually wrote accepted the invitation: the refusal is the novel’s, and the note should say so.
candidates.speaker: Sido, the narrator’s mother, declining her son in law’s invitation
candidates.whyThisMonth: A refusal in favour of a flowering: the one appointment that cannot be moved is the plant’s, once in four years, and the month is about exactly that.

candidates.quote: Travel is in my opinion a very profitable exercise; the soul is there continually employed in observing new and unknown things, and I do not know, as I have often said a better school wherein to model life than by incessantly exposing to it the diversity of so many other lives, fancies, and usances, and by making it relish a perpetual variety of forms of human nature.
candidates.author: Michel de Montaigne
candidates.work: Essays, Book III, chapter IX, Of Vanity
candidates.locator: Book III, chapter IX, Of Vanity, in the paragraph beginning Besides these reasons; The Essays of Montaigne, trans. Charles Cotton, ed. William Carew Hazlitt, read in Project Gutenberg 3600. The quotation drops Cotton’s opening Besides these reasons and capitalises travel; the missing comma after said is Hazlitt’s text and not a slip. Donald Frame’s 1958 English of the same sentence is the better known.
candidates.whyThisMonth: The second half of the month’s theme in one sentence: the road is a school, and the subject is other people’s ways of being alive.
candidates.translator: Charles Cotton, 1685, in W. C. Hazlitt’s revision of 1877

candidates.quote: To awaken quite alone in a strange town is one of the pleasantest sensations in the world. You are surrounded by adventure. You have no idea of what is in store for you, but you will, if you are wise and know the art of travel, let yourself go on the stream of the unknown and accept whatever comes in the spirit in which the gods may offer it.
candidates.author: Freya Stark
candidates.locator: The opening of the sketch In the Moslem Quarter, p. 17 of the John Murray edition (1937), read in the archive.org scan in.ernet.dli.2015.81846; first published by the Times Press, Baghdad, 1932. Every quotation book drops the of in no idea of what is in store, and most stop after the first sentence; the Murray page has been read and carries all three.
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is a waking line before it is a travel line, and it tells the reader what to do with a day whose contents are not yet known.

candidates.quote: Those who contemplate the beauty of the earth find reserves of strength that will endure as long as life lasts. There is symbolic as well as actual beauty in the migration of the birds, the ebb and flow of the tides, the folded bud ready for the spring. There is something infinitely healing in the repeated refrains of nature—the assurance that dawn comes after night, and spring after the winter.
candidates.author: Rachel Carson
candidates.locator: The closing pages; The Sense of Wonder (Harper and Row, 1965), read in the Perennial Library printing at pp. 88 to 89, where the page break falls inside the last sentence (archive.org scan senseofwonder0000cars_d2s9). First published as the article Help Your Child to Wonder, Woman’s Home Companion, July 1956. The dash before the assurance is the printed text’s own.
candidates.whyThisMonth: Dawn after night and spring after winter, stated by a scientist rather than a comforter, is the renewal the whole month rests on.
candidates.year: 1956 as an article; 1965 as a book

candidates.quote: Yet often the mountain gives itself most completely when I have no destination, when I reach nowhere in particular, but have gone out merely to be with the mountain as one visits a friend with no intention but to be with him.
candidates.author: Nan Shepherd
candidates.locator: Chapter 2, The Recesses, p. 15 of the Canongate edition (2011), a few lines after the sentence on those who want the startling view, the horrid pinnacle; first published by Aberdeen University Press in 1977 and read in the archive.org scan of the 1984 Aberdeen printing (bwb_KR-674-517). The chapter and page come from a reader’s citation of the Canongate text and should be seen on the page before landing.
candidates.whyThisMonth: The correction the month needs: the way gives most when it is not being used to arrive anywhere, which is worth knowing before the day’s list starts.
